title: Algorithms at medium scale
summary: A GHZ state on 12 logical qubits in 359 physical qubits at distance 3, Deutsch–Jozsa on 13 logical qubits in 379 physical qubits at distance 3, a GHZ state on 6 logical qubits in 419 physical qubits at distance 5, Bernstein–Vazirani on 17 logical qubits in 480 physical qubits at distance 3, teleportation on 16 logical qubits in 429 physical qubits at distance 3, Deutsch–Jozsa on 9 logical qubits in 652 physical qubits at distance 5 and a GHZ state on 10 logical qubits in 699 physical qubits at distance 5, each run through the operating system's interface on a superconducting machine whose control system spans 91, 80, 111, 100, 100, 157 and 186 boards.
method: Each algorithm is a logical program. The fault-tolerant compiler lowers it to a QSysASM listing of system calls against the machine's system specification, and its resource VM admits the listing. The OS then executes every system call at its listed time on the control system, and durations the hardware needed enter the next specification until every call fits its window.

The machine is a generated superconducting chip, one transmon per RISC-Q control core, two 4-core decoders, 16,384 words of RAM per core, placed on as many AMD ZCU216 boards as it needs. Every core runs firmware compiled from the listing in the cycle-exact model of RISC-Q; boards exchange measured bits and barriers over their PutLanes.

sections.heading: The programs
sections.text: GHZ state on 12 logical qubits: 12 blocks in |+⟩ joined by a chain of Z⊗Z lattice-surgery merges into a 12-qubit GHZ state, then read out in Z. Deutsch–Jozsa on 12 inputs: 12 inputs in |+⟩ and a target in |−⟩; a balanced oracle f(x) = s·x (s = 101101101101₂) applied as lattice-surgery CNOTs from each input of s onto the target; the inputs read out in X give s, so f is balanced. GHZ state on 6 logical qubits at distance 5: 6 blocks of the distance-5 surface code in |+⟩ joined by Z⊗Z lattice-surgery merges into a GHZ state, then read out in Z. Bernstein–Vazirani on 16 inputs: The hidden string s = 1011001110001101₂ of the oracle f(x) = s·x, found with one query: 16 inputs in |+⟩ and a target in |−⟩, a lattice-surgery CNOT from each input where s has a 1, then the inputs read out in X, which give s. It is the Deutsch–Jozsa circuit with a linear oracle; Bernstein–Vazirani asks for s itself. Teleportation along 16 logical qubits: A logical |+⟩ teleported block to block along a chain of 16: each step prepares the next block in |+⟩, merges the two by Z⊗Z lattice surgery and measures the old block in X; the two outcomes set the next block's X and Z frame corrections. The last block, read out in X, gives +. Deutsch–Jozsa on 8 inputs at distance 5: 8 inputs and a target in blocks of the distance-5 surface code; the balanced oracle f(x) = s·x (s = 10110101₂) as lattice-surgery CNOTs onto the target; the inputs read out in X give s, so f is balanced. GHZ state on 10 logical qubits at distance 5: 10 blocks of the distance-5 surface code in |+⟩ joined by Z⊗Z lattice-surgery merges into a GHZ state, then read out in Z.

findings: The largest run, GHZ state on 10 logical qubits at distance 5, uses 699 physical qubits and 708 control cores on 186 boards.
Every system call of every program ran inside its window.
The longest derivation, from compile to a specification every call fits, took 32 minutes on one workstation.

note: All numbers are measured on QuantumOS's Lean model of RISC-Q control hardware (its cores, hubs and lanes are checked against RISC-Q's RTL cycle for cycle), on generated or published hardware designs. They are properties of that model, not of laboratory hardware.
